segments.text: Imagine two people starting in similar roles.
They have similar abilities, similar opportunities,
and similar support.
One comes to work, does what is required,
finishes the day, and repeats the same pattern.
The other asks, what do I want to be better at
six months from now?
What skill do I want to develop?
What would make me more capable, more effective,
and more useful to the team?
A year later, those two people may be
in very different places.
Why?
Because one simply worked.
The other worked with direction.
Goals help you take ownership of your growth.
Other people can give you training, feedback, support,
and opportunities to learn,
but no one can take responsibility
for your development for you.
That part belongs to you.
Maybe you want to become more confident in your role.
Maybe you want to communicate more clearly.
Maybe you want to become more efficient.
Maybe you want to solve problems more independently.
Maybe you want to develop a new skill,
improve how you organize your work,
or understand another part of the organization.
Without a goal, these ambitions
often remain good intentions.
A goal turns those intentions into a clear direction.
One of the biggest mistakes we make
is confusing a wish with a goal.
I want to get better at my job.
I want to communicate better.
I want to be more organized.
Those are good intentions, but they are still too vague.
A goal creates clarity instead of saying,
I want to get better at my job.
You might say, over the next 90 days,
I want to develop one new skill
that makes me more capable and independent in my role.
Instead of saying, I want to communicate better.
You might say, for the next three months,
I will focus on giving clearer updates,
asking better questions,
and making sure people understand what they need from me.
When a goal is clear, you can act on it.
Once you know your goal, work backwards.
Ask yourself, where do I want to be six months from now?
Then, what would I need to improve over the next 90 days?
Then, what should I work on this week?
And finally, what can I do today?
If your goal is to become more confident in your role,
today's action might be asking someone experience
to show you how they approach a difficult task.
If your goal is to become more efficient,
today's action might simply be looking at something
you do repeatedly and asking,
is there a better way to do this?
Big goals become manageable.
When you turn them into small actions,
you cannot control every outcome,
but you can control how you grow.
You can become more skilled, more reliable,
more efficient, more adaptable.
You can communicate better.
You can learn faster.
You can become better at solving problems.
You can become someone others trust and depend on.
This is where goal setting becomes powerful.
Do not focus only on what you hope will happen.
Set goals around the skills, habits and behaviors
you can actually develop
because those things are in your hands.
Growth does not have to mean changing roles.
Growth can mean becoming better
at the role you already have.
More skilled, more efficient, more reliable,
more knowledgeable, more adaptable,
more capable of solving problems.
It might mean learning about another part of the organization.
It might mean improving how you communicate.
It might mean making fewer mistakes,
finding a better way to complete a repeated task
or becoming someone people can depend on
when something needs to get done.
Wherever you are in the organization,
there is always another level you can develop.
The question is, what do I want to become better at next?
What happens if you do not reach your goal?
It does not mean the goal was pointless.
It means you now have information to work with.
Maybe you were not consistent.
Maybe the goal was too ambitious.
Maybe the plan was not clear enough.
Maybe something changed along the way.
The important thing is to review what happened.
Ask, what worked?
What did not?
What did I learn?
What will I change?
Then adjust your plan and continue.
A goal is not a test of whether you are good enough.
It is a tool that helps you grow.
The goal is not perfection.
The goal is progress.
So here is your challenge.
Choose one area where you want to grow.
Maybe it is a skill, communication, efficiency,
problem solving, organization, leadership,
technical ability, or learning something completely new.
Write down one clear goal.
Then ask yourself, why does this matter?
What would success look like 90 days from now?
What can I do this week?
And most importantly, what can I do today?
Do not wait for someone else to decide
what you should become better at.
Take ownership of your growth.
Wherever you are in the organization,
keep asking, what can I learn?
What can I improve?
What can I become better at next?
The people who grow the most are not always
the people who started with the most experience.
They are often the people who decided
where they wanted to improve and kept working towards it.
Set the direction.
Then take the next step.
